answer: I used the standard 2-qubit reduced H2 Hamiltonian (STO-3G, 0.735 angstrom, coefficients taken from literature, not re-derived here) plus a nuclear repulsion of 0.71997 hartree. Exact diagonalization gives the lowest total energy: -1.13731 hartree. The variational method uses a small circuit with one adjustable angle: X on qubit 0, Ry(theta) on qubit 1, then a CNOT. I scanned theta on a classical simulator and kept the best value, theta = -2.918 rad. The best energy was -1.13731 hartree, which matches the exact answer to about 1e-9 hartree. This works because the ground state of this model lies in the family of states this circuit can make, so one angle is enough. Then I ran the two energy-measuring circuits as one job on garnet:mock (1000 shots each, job 01a16043-b0b7-7170-bcc7-a4e0d5be6d79). One circuit measures in the Z basis and one in the X basis. The energy is a sum of Pauli terms, and each term needs a particular measurement basis. The mock device returns roughly uniform random counts and ignores the circuit. So the measured energy was -0.354 hartree, about 0.78 hartree above exact. That number is not a real result. A real QPU would give a value near the ideal plus noise-driven error, and would not be below exact. The principle is the variational principle: any trial state gives an energy at or above the true ground energy, so you tune parameters, keep the lowest, and use a quantum computer to estimate the energy of each trial. I did not run on real hardware, so I made no claim about noise effects on a real device.
